walkthroughs.body_html:
Introduction to Economics — a core area of GCSE Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Introduction to Economics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Introduction to Economics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a factor of production?
options: Land
Labour
Money
Enterprise
The price of bread
The whole economy
A single firm's profits
A consumer's choices

mcqs.q: What is the difference between CPI and RPI as inflation measures?
options: CPI and RPI always give the same inflation figure.
CPI measures consumer prices and RPI measures retail prices — that's the only difference.

Both measure price changes via a basket of goods, but RPI includes housing costs (mortgage interest) and uses an arithmetic mean; CPI excludes housing costs and uses a geometric mean — CPI is the official UK target measure.
A public good is anything that's free.

mcqs.q: How is economic growth shown on a Production Possibility Curve?
options: CPI measures consumer prices and RPI measures retail prices — that's the only difference.
Growth is shown by the curve becoming straighter.
By an outward shift of the entire curve — reflecting an increase in productive capacity through more or better resources, technology, or skills.
Growth is shown by moving from inside the curve to a point on the curve.

mcqs.q: What defines a pure public good?
options: A public good is anything that's free.
Non-rivalry (one person's use doesn't reduce others') and non-excludability (you can't stop people benefiting) — e.g. national defence, street lighting.
Growth is shown by the curve becoming straighter.
A public good is anything provided by the government.
